opus-5.5.text:
I think what's really appealing is that these models come with a huge amount of world knowledge that we simply can't get from our own driving data alone. They've been trained on internet-scale image and text data, so they already have a sense of what a lot of things are and how they relate to each other. They know what an ambulance looks like, what a construction zone is, what it means when a police officer is waving you through, or that a person carrying a stop sign is a crossing guard. In autonomous driving, a lot of the hard problems are in the long tail: rare objects, unusual situations, things you might see once in millions of miles. Labeling enough examples of all of those to train a classic supervised detector is very expensive and sometimes just not feasible.

With vision-language models, you get a much richer and more open-vocabulary representation. Instead of a fixed taxonomy of, say, vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists and a few other classes, you can start to describe the scene in language and reason about semantic attributes, intent, and context. That helps with understanding, and it also helps with things like data mining. You can search through your logs for "a mattress on the highway" or "a child chasing a ball" without having built a dedicated classifier for each.

The other appealing part is generalization and transfer. These models are a strong foundation that you can adapt and distill into the onboard system, so you benefit from that pretraining while still meeting the latency and safety requirements of a real-time stack. The challenge, of course, is that out of the box they aren't designed for precise 3D geometry, multi-sensor fusion with lidar and radar, or the reliability we need. So the interesting work is combining their semantic knowledge with the spatial precision and rigor that driving demands.

r001.rationale: The response says the models bring broad pretrained knowledge, enabling open-vocabulary understanding and searches for rare concepts without a dedicated classifier or extensive labeled examples for each.

r002.rationale: It mentions generalization and internet-scale pretraining, but does not state that increasing model scale improves generalization to unfamiliar visual variants.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What's most appealing to me is that these models bring world knowledge into perception in a way we never had before. For a long time, autonomous driving perception was built on fairly narrow, task-specific models. You'd train a detector on labeled data for cars, pedestrians, cyclists, and it would do well on those categories, but it had essentially no notion of anything outside that closed set. If you encountered something rare, say a mattress on the freeway or a construction worker waving a hand-painted sign, the model had no prior to lean on. It might detect "an obstacle," but it couldn't reason about what it was or how it might behave.

Vision-language models change that. Because they've been trained on an enormous breadth of internet-scale image and text data, they come in already knowing what a mattress is, what a police officer directing traffic looks like, that a ball rolling into the street is often followed by a child. That semantic understanding of the long tail is exactly the hard part of driving. The common cases we've handled well for years. It's the rare, weird situations that determine whether you can actually deploy at scale, and those are precisely where world knowledge matters most.

The second thing I find compelling is the language interface itself. It gives you a natural way to query the model, to ask it to explain a scene, to describe what's unusual, to reason about intent. That's useful for the system, but it's also useful for us as engineers. Instead of training a separate classifier for every new concept, you can describe the concept in words and evaluate immediately. It makes the whole development loop faster and much more flexible.

And finally there's the unification aspect. Historically we had a lot of specialized components, each with its own representation. A large multimodal model offers a shared foundation that can be adapted across tasks, and that pretrained prior means you need far less driving-specific data to get strong performance on a new problem. At Waymo this is a big part of why we've been investing in these models, bringing that general capability together with the very specific, safety-critical requirements of driving.

r001.rationale: The response says engineers can describe a new concept in words and evaluate it without training a separate classifier for it, communicating perception of concepts without explicit concept-specific labels.

r002.rationale: It links broad internet-scale pretraining with world knowledge about rare situations, but does not state that increasing model scale improves generalization to unfamiliar visual variants.

astra-6.text:
What I find appealing is the breadth of what they can recognize and describe. In a traditional perception system, you define a set of categories, collect labeled data, and train a model to identify those categories. But the world is much richer than any taxonomy you can write down, particularly when you’re driving. You encounter unusual objects, unusual situations, and interactions that are difficult to capture with a fixed set of labels.

Vision-language models give us a way to tap into much broader knowledge and to ask questions about a scene in natural language. It’s not just, “Is there a vehicle here?” You can start asking, “What kind of situation is this? What is unusual about it?” That’s exciting both for building richer representations and for helping us discover and understand interesting cases in our data.

Of course, being able to describe an image convincingly isn’t the same as having the precise, reliable understanding you need for driving. Spatial accuracy, motion, and consistency over time still matter enormously. The opportunity is to bring that broad semantic understanding together with the rigor of a perception system that has to operate in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts fixed labeled categories with broader natural-language scene understanding, but it does not clearly state that these models bootstrap perception without explicit labels for particular concepts.

r002.rationale: The response says the models recognize a broad range and handle unusual cases, but it does not connect improved generalization to increasing model scale.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s appealing is the breadth of what these models can recognize and understand. In a traditional perception system, you define a set of categories, collect labeled data, and train the model to identify those categories. But in driving, the world keeps presenting things you didn’t explicitly plan for.

Vision-language models offer a way to bring much broader knowledge into that process. You can describe something in language and ask the model to find it, or ask questions about a scene that go beyond a fixed set of object labels. That’s exciting both for understanding unusual situations and for helping us discover and annotate examples in our data.

Of course, recognizing something in an image is only part of the problem. For driving, you also need precise geometry, motion, and consistent understanding over time. So the opportunity is to combine that broad semantic understanding with the precision and reliability a driving system needs.
